entities.summary:
Morgan Stanley, founded in 1935 in New York by Henry S. Morgan (grandson of J.P. Morgan) and Harold Stanley — who both resigned from J.P. Morgan & Co. in response to the Glass-Steagall Act of 1933 that required the separation of commercial and investment banking — is one of the world's leading global investment banks and financial services companies, managing approximately $5-6 trillion in client assets and consistently ranked among the world's most systemically important financial institutions.

Morgan Stanley's founding was a direct consequence of New Deal financial regulation: the Glass-Steagall Act (Banking Act of 1933), passed in response to the 1929 crash and Depression, prohibited commercial banks from underwriting securities. J.P. Morgan & Co. chose to remain a commercial bank, leading Morgan and Stanley to leave and create a dedicated investment bank. Morgan Stanley's first-day underwriting ($1.1 billion in 1935 dollars) reflected the enormous investment banking demand that Glass-Steagall's separation had created.

The firm's 20th-century trajectory included major corporate bond and equity underwriting, the growth of its institutional sales and trading divisions, and the 1986 decision to go public. Its 2008 financial crisis near-collapse (liquidity crisis following Lehman Brothers' failure) required Federal Reserve emergency lending and a $9 billion investment by Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group — transforming it into a bank holding company. Post-crisis Morgan Stanley has refocused on wealth management (the 2009 acquisition of Smith Barney from Citigroup and the 2020 acquisition of E*Trade) making it one of the world's largest wealth management firms alongside its investment banking operations.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Morgan Stanley — born from New Deal regulation, managing trillions in global assets, surviving the 2008 financial crisis with Federal Reserve emergency support, and pivoting to become one of the world's largest wealth managers — is one of the most systemically important financial institutions in global capitalism.
